speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In particular, financial technology (fintech) has opened up opportunities for more convenient, faster and cheaper payments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, new payment methods give rise to new risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This has necessitated a review of our regulatory framework.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, services that were previously provided separately and regulated separately are now merging.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) currently regulates various types of payment services under two Acts, first, the 2006 Payment Systems (Oversight) Act, or PS(O)A, and the 1979 Money-Changing and Remittance Businesses Act (MCRBA).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Payment Services Bill provides a forward-looking and flexible framework for the regulation of payment systems and payment service providers in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It provides for regulatory certainty and consumer safeguards, while encouraging innovation and growth of payment services and fintech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In drafting the Bill, MAS has taken reference from regulatory frameworks in various other financial centres – Australia, Hong Kong, Japan and the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, we are adopting a regulatory structure that recognises the growing convergence across payment activities which I just mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, payment and remittance services are now often provided as one product to customers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, we are expanding MAS’ regulatory scope to include more types of payment services, such as digital payment token services and merchant acquisition.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill includes provisions that level the playing field for banks and non-banks, and that enhances user protection.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, we have adopted a modular and risk-focused regulatory structure, so that our rules are tailored to the scope of services being offered by any provider.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A modular approach gives MAS the flexibility to regulate payment service providers that offer one, two or more parts of the payment value chain.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It also enables MAS to respond quickly to fast-changing payment solutions and business models.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A risk-based approach enables MAS to impose proportionate regulatory measures on each type of payment service provider, depending on the scale of their activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has conducted public consultations on the Bill and has engaged extensively with the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has considered all the feedback and, where appropriate, has taken them into account in preparing this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill comprises two regulatory frameworks: a designation regime and a licensing regime.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The designation regime enables MAS to designate significant payment systems to ensure the stability and market efficiency of the financial system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Designating payment systems for financial stability reasons is a power that is already provided under the PS(O)A, and that will be retained.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, the Bill provides for an additional basis for designation, which is to ensure efficiency and competition in the financial system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is because a payment system that becomes widely used and dominant can be used to shut out competition and new, innovative players.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, for competition reasons, MAS can designate a payment system if it is widely used in Singapore, or its operations have an impact on the operations of other payment systems in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second framework is quite a complex one.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a licensing regime to allow MAS to regulate a wide range of payment services in a manner that matches the scope and scale of services provided by each provider, and that can respond flexibly to market developments, as I have explained.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Service providers may offer different combinations of these services, and the licensing regime will regulate them according to the risks they pose.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will not impose requirements uniformly across all licensed payment service providers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These three classes will be broad enough to deal with the different combinations of payment services that a service provider may offer.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Each service provider needs to hold only one of the three licences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And in line with our risk-based approach, the regulatory requirements for each class of licence differ according to the risks posed by the scope and scale of services provided by the licensee.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, money-changing licensees can provide only money-changing services.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will continue to be regulated under the Bill in largely the same way as it is under the existing MCRBA, as the attendant risks have not changed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The regulation is quite narrow in scope, as these are over-the-counter services often offered by small businesses, such as sole proprietors, with limited risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will be regulated more lightly, and the regime mimics a “permanent sandbox” environment to encourage innovation and enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, this is where fintech companies will play.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, major payment institutions can go above the specified thresholds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the scale of their operations would pose more risk, they will be subject to more regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This new licensing regime is a more comprehensive and robust framework than what current legislation provides.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will be regulating new services, as well as expanding the scope of activities under the services we currently regulate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will be among the first few financial services regulators in the world to introduce a regulatory framework for DPT services, and this is more commonly understood as cryptocurrency dealing or exchange services, but we call it DPT in this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we have stated in Parliament before, while there may be some potential in these DPT services, they also carry significant money laundering and terrorism financing risks (ML/TF risks) due to the anonymous and borderless nature of the transactions they enable.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will be using more of that later; so, just to be clear.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also recognising new activities under the services we currently regulate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The definition of e-money in the Bill will go beyond stored value or prepaid services, such as public transport cards, to include, now, e-wallets, that is, any monetary value that is held for future payment transfers between individuals or with corporates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means that e-money issuers have an obligation to protect the value held in major e-wallets for consumers and merchants.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, under the Bill, we will regulate inward remittance services in addition to outbound remittance services that are currently regulated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Bill will also clarify that a person will be presumed to carry on a business of providing a payment service even where the payment service is only incidental to the person’s primary business.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The intent is to dis-apply the 2017 Singapore High Court decision in Chinpo Shipping Co (Pte) Ltd v Public Prosecutor, which suggests that the undertaking of remittances that are purely incidental to a primary business of ship agency and ship chandelling would not have constituted the carrying on of a remittance business under the MCRBA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Proper oversight of these risks will both protect the public and facilitate a vibrant payment services sector.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The first key risk is that customer monies entrusted to payment service providers may be lost, such as when the service provider becomes insolvent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, we also want to ensure that measures are not too onerous or stifling.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we adopted three classes of licences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, for example, standard payment institutions are not subject to the safeguarding requirements which are for major payment institutions, but the standard payment institutions must disclose this to their customers so that the customers can make informed decisions on which payment service or provider best suits their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second risk is that payment services may be used for ML/TF, such as through illicit cross-border transfers, anonymous cash-based payment transactions, structuring of payments to avoid reporting thresholds or the raising or layering of assets or funds for ML/TF purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS studies the business model of each payment service to determine where regulatory measures should be imposed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The appropriate AML/CFT requirements will be imposed on relevant licensees through Notices issued under the MAS Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS will also provide guidance to the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A third risk is that payment solutions in Singapore become fragmented.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have deliberately allowed many e-payment solutions to come on stream in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the downside is that it can also be confusing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MAS has been persuading the industry to undertake various measures to ensure that the solutions are interoperable within an open architecture.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example, we worked with the banks to implement PayNow to make instant payment transfers more convenient for consumers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, today, I can use the PayNow feature from the app of one bank to pay a friend who is banking with a different institution.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the money I transfer goes directly into his bank account, and that is open architecture interoperability at work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also worked with the industry to introduce the Singapore Quick Response (SGQR) 	Code, which allows different e-payment schemes to be accepted via a single standardised and unified QR code.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This Bill will give MAS formal powers to ensure interoperability of payment solutions in the interests of consumers and market development.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will continue to employ its powers of persuasion with the payment players before using its interoperability powers as a last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will require payment service providers to ensure there is adequate risk governance and implementation of adequate controls, particularly in areas, such as user authentication, data loss protection and cyberattack prevention and detection.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means tailoring our regulations to the activities of the licensees, such as opening accounts, issuing e-money, transferring money within Singapore and overseas, and providing e-payment solutions to consumers and merchants.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It must, therefore, follow that if the licensees wish to do more, then they must be subject to more regulatory measures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Licensees, therefore, cannot engage in consumer lending or banking activities, such as accepting deposits and granting loans, unless they hold the appropriate licence under the Banking Act or the Moneylenders Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Banks perform a vital economic function of intermediating savings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They take in deposits and on-lend these funds back into the economy to help it grow.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To protect depositors' interests, banks are subject to much more stringent prudential regulation and supervision, such as on the amount of capital and liquid assets they must hold, how much concentration risk they can take, and how they manage repayment risks and make provisions against those risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Non-bank payment service licensees do not perform similar economic functions, and do not face similarly stringent regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Additionally, withdrawals of Singapore dollars will not be allowed from e-money accounts held by Singapore residents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is consistent with the objective of the Bill, which is to promote greater adoption of electronic payments, in lieu of cash services.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will also preserve the privileges of our Free Trade Agreement partners, whose banks have been accorded access to automated teller machines and cashback services.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will also be subject to an annual flow cap.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is the maximum cumulative amount of yearly outflows from the personal payment account, other than to the user's designated bank accounts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These caps will not apply to merchant payment accounts that cater to business uses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These caps help to further protect customers by limiting a customer's potential loss from his e-money account.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This also enables the e-money safeguarding measures to be simple and low-cost, different from deposit insurance that banks have to undertake.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will help us build a technologically robust smart financial centre that preserves stability while facilitating innovation and growth in the payments landscape.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With more services going cashless, we have seen an increase in the number of payment services and activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To maintain our reputation as a global financial hub and to facilitate smooth transactions, we have to keep up with these changes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Meanwhile, these changes also bring along with them new risks, so we must stay vigilant and guard against these risks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will, in turn, lead to greater confidence and more widespread use of e-payment services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Overall, not only will we expect a more secure environment for all to conduct transactions, we can also look forward to increased innovation in payment services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a Bill which I foresee will be followed up by more amendments in the near future as the payment services landscape continues to evolve and grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although it is important to adopt international standards and guidelines, it would be unwise to adopt a reactive stand and wait for these guidelines to be finalised.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One feedback is that the banks have shut their doors to the virtual currency industry.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many, including digital exchanges, have had their bank accounts closed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: New applications were rejected according to the Digital Exchange Association protem committee members, whom I had the opportunity of having a focus group discussion with.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also note that late last year, MAS expressed readiness in helping cryptocurrency firms to set up local bank accounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, on the digital banking licence, I understand that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority has a much more liberal approach and they were considering giving approval to allow some cryptocurrency firms to conduct banking activity, including taking deposits and lending.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps the Minister could clarify if Singapore is looking into issuance of digital banking licences to such firms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we are to position ourselves as a fintech hub, doing so would help to improve financial inclusion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another issue is whether there could be more transparency by requiring payment providers to disclose the fees charged, what benefit the payment providers benefit from on-selling of any third-party products, and whether these providers are related to parties in a transaction.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, on the regulation of Crypto Custodians, whether MAS is considering this so that the man-in-the-street is protected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are the businesses which hold the monies of their customers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Should there be guidelines like what percentage of customers assets should be kept in "hot" or "cold" wallets?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These days, many of us use e-services that come with their own e-wallet, where consumers can deposit money in advance so it is ready on the go.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But while convenient, problems like system errors and hacking incidents mean that consumers should be wary of incurring possible losses as a result.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the e-payment company goes out of business, this money is also not protected.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, to avoid stifling innovation and advent of new payment services, the smaller payment services providers are not subjected to the same requirements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Instead, they would be required to inform their customers that their monies are not subjected to safeguarding requirements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciate the Minister's intentions to encourage smaller, experimental companies to set up and establish their businesses here.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Certainly, being less rigid towards the newer players has its benefits and will help the e-payment industry grow.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Nevertheless, it will be necessary to establish a set of mandatory policies on how such advisories should be administered.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Certainly, it would be inappropriate to put the advisory in small print in the terms and conditions, which many people already do not read or find difficult to comprehend.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The advisory must be published somewhere easily visible and it should be accompanied by further explanations on the risks involved.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Furthermore, I think that these smaller payment service providers should still be required to set aside a deposit, in lesser amount than that of the major payment service providers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sometimes, when a company has to undergo insolvency, it leaves behind some issues that take up additional resources to resolve.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the Land Transport Authority had to impound bikes and follow up with Mobike to ensure their bikes are removed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The monies from the fund can be used to fund such operations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, I believe it will help to hold these companies to greater accountability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Experiential and risk-taking behaviour should be encouraged, but when large sums of money from the public are involved, one cannot afford to be too free with it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Several big players have earlier expressed disagreement with the cap amounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Alipay, Wirecard and Paypal have said that the caps will slow down the growth of e-payments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And this is understandable as these are reputable companies often dealing with high value goods and services as well as the remittance of large amounts of money and purchase of investment products.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Minister has said in his speech that these caps will not be applicable to merchant payment accounts that cater to business uses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I think that this should put to rest some of the concerns expressed by the payment service providers, there are personal accounts that frequently deal with larger figures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, some companies already have safeguards in place for dealing with higher amounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we want to manage the pace of deposit outflows and safeguard financial stability and limit potential losses, we also do not want to stifle businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the near future, I believe we can only expect more businesses to introduce their own apps and payment services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This means transactions will go up in value, and these caps, while adequate now, may become too prohibitive in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having a number of different payment platforms can lead to increased inconvenience and frustration.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: No one wants their smartphones to be filled with e-wallets and payment apps, which no doubt takes up precious storage space, as we all probably know.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A multitude of apps to choose from also means more confusion over payments, especially for the older users.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The decision to mandate participation of a common payment platform and common standard is an important move.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It allows for payment systems to be interoperable, as what Minister has mentioned just now, and makes e-payments more user-friendly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have a question: what is the Ministry's forecast on our progress with regard to this aspect?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How soon can we expect to move to this common platform?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the affected merchants expect any assistance from the Ministry or MAS for that matter?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The regulatory focus will be on ML/TF, as the Minister has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But such regulations will give cryptocurrency players more clarity and confidence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The feedback from the ground is that regulations are welcomed by local players and gives more confidence to the market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will these regulations also serve as a positive signal to the overseas fintech industry in terms of our openness to see more of such activities on our shores?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the current regulations do not cover user protection for public use of virtual currency, what are the Minister's plans for a public consultation to formulate relevant policies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the recent Group of 20 (G20) meeting last year, country leaders have called for international cryptocurrency taxation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a testament to how fast the industry is moving globally, and a sign that we need to step up on further regulations in terms of personal transactions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that Singapore's MAS has been fully supportive of the G20 and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I hope that as we make new rules and impositions on our financial institutions and others, we do not impose too much a burden on them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Jobs are among the main benefits that would come from the diversification of the financial sector, and the development of the fintech sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In enhancing our licensing framework, we must ensure that it does not inhibit overseas businesses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To stay accessible to overseas markets, it would also be prudent to keep up with the international standards so that we maintain our reputation as a safe yet convenient place to do business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My last point is with regard to exclusions and royalty points.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note with concern some exclusions from licensing under the Bill, namely, limited purpose e-money, incidental payment services by licensed entities, and loyalty programmes and limited purpose virtual currency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And some of these things are practically being traded like cash on online forums and selling platforms for a profit.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, unlike regular goods and services, these items are partial or full substitutes for currency payments on specific platforms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One potential abuse problem I see with regard to virtual currency is that underaged users would purchase in-game assets through other platforms because they do not have credit cards.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, Sir, the MAS currently regulates the various types of payment services under two Acts, namely, the PS(O)A and the MCRBA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill covers a whole gamut of activities, including money changing and cross-border transfers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill proposes a dual-track regulatory framework, one intended for major payment institutions, while the other is intended for smaller players.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a PricewaterhouseCoopers report put it, the approach is a "broadening of the licensing regime for payments activities to create certainty for a wider spectrum of payment services providers" and "a departure from a product-based licensing model towards a more flexible activities-based and risk-based licensing model".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, Sir, before I proceed, I declare my interest as the Chief Executive Officer of a research consultancy that undertakes studies in financial services, among other industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do, however, have a number of clarifications to seek.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does this mean that such payment service providers are only prohibited from earning interest or other income from providing credit services, or does this extend to such service providers being prohibited from, for example, allowing very short-term, small-scale overdraft to be run on e-wallets at zero interest?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will payment service providers, including standard payment licensees as well as exempt payment licensees, so to speak, be required to provide such explanations to their customers and will the requirement be sufficiently prescriptive in terms of the language used?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One reason I ask this is because clause 13 states that persons may apply to be exempt from many of the provisions of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One issue facing users of electronic financial services is that explanation of risks is often couched in very wordy, arcane and legalistic language – risks, such as, for example, that e-money floats are not safeguarded by MAS regulations for standard payment services licensees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would payment service providers be encouraged and required to make available simple and clear risk statements, for example, available with one click on a typical user interface?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said that, I do acknowledge that the longer and legally comprehensive statements also have to be provided and acknowledged by customers alongside such simpler summaries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask what measures are in place to promote greater financial literacy among customers of financial services in relation to the risks associated with e-money and virtual currencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 4.8 of the MAS consultation paper read: "A standard Payment Institution that wishes to upgrade its licence to a Major Payment Institution Licence will need to apply for a variation of licence before the thresholds are breached." I understand that MAS did address this issue in point 4.8 of its consultation response paper.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would just seek to clarify if, as was suggested in that response, payment service providers that realise they have breached the thresholds would be required to apply for an upgrade of their licence by a set date every year as part of an annual licence review cycle; or, instead, would be given a fixed period of grace time to make that application from the time when there is evidence that the threshold was breached?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Section 3.15 in the consultation response paper states that cash withdrawal is not allowed because the aim of this Bill is not to promote cash and also because of restrictions imposed by Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) that require this to be the exclusive provenance of qualifying full banks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it would appear that withdrawals of non-Singapore dollars and by non-Singapore residents are exempt.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not clear why the latter is permitted and the former is not, since withdrawals of non-Singapore dollars and by non-Singapore residents may also raise similar AML and CFT concerns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would MAS consider allowing limited withdrawals of cash from stored value balances up to a maximum cap to limit the AML and CFT downside risk and to the extent that it is FTA-compliant, so as to increase convenience for users of stored value balances who, for various reasons, may feel it necessary to use small amounts of cash for day-to-day expenses purposes?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifthly, this Bill regulates virtual currency intermediaries for AML and CFT purposes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask if MAS is monitoring the ownership and attitudes towards virtual currency domestically, so as to be in a better position to judge when interventions are advisable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There could potentially be demand from some customer segments for larger e-money transaction sizes using e-wallets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These caps could limit the scope for new entrepreneurial business models emerging catering to these segments, which could, in theory, scale up their business overseas and create good jobs for Singaporeans to support such export sales.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A minimum annual taxable income floor could also apply to those customers where caps are raised, to protect the most vulnerable group of customers.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to speak on the Bill.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to focus on the consumer protections that will be strengthened with this Bill.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These measures will help to boost consumer confidence in e-payments and give our fintech sector a further shot in the arm.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Over three decades ago, in March 1985, the Government launched the National Campaign to Minimise Cash Transactions to urge Singaporeans to undertake more financial transactions electronically, so as to increase productivity, reduce costs and make cashless transactions a way of life.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This three-month campaign successfully convinced more Singaporeans to switch to receiving their salaries through direct credit to the bank, pay bills electronically via General Interbank Recurring Order (GIRO), and make purchases through the Electronic Funds Transfer at Point of Sale service.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: With that historical context in mind, we need to ask why Singapore is not even further ahead in realising our vision of a cashless society.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: While Singapore is widely regarded as a fintech hub, it is also common to hear observations that we lag behind our regional neighbours in areas, such as mobile payment.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Our relatively slower adoption of mobile payment is somewhat anomalous, considering Singapore's early embrace of cashless payments.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Being a first mover can, indeed, be a mixed blessing.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Precisely because of our more mature financial ecosystem, consumers are well-accustomed to, and very well-served by the Network for Electronic Transfers (NETS) and credit cards.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The relative advantage of newer e-payment systems is thus not as significantly felt.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Cash is also the favoured payment option for small-value transactions, such as in hawker centres, convenience stores and taxis.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of automated cash collection machines in hawker centres and supermarkets may also further entrench our reliance on cash.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the benefits of going cashless are considerable.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In many respects, therefore, e-payments are eminently superior and we must zero in on the probable causes of consumer resistance to the newer e-payment services out there.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard concerns, even from acquaintances in their 20s and 30s, that they do not use e-wallets or mobile payment because they are not confident of their security or reliability.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, the results of PayPal's "Digital Payments: Thinking Beyond Transactions" survey released in August 2017 found that 51% of Singapore consumers surveyed expressed privacy concerns.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Sixty-three percent said that more payment methods meant more confusion for consumers, and 53% found it challenging to keep up with fast-moving digital trends.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, there is also feedback that e-payment interfaces should be much more intuitive so that they can help speed up transactions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, some e-payment methods involve several steps that may yet require more time per transaction than by just paying with good old cash.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Overall, there is also the problem of too many e-payment platforms and choices, and we need to accelerate systems integration to overcome the current fragmentation.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: So, I welcome the Minister's assurance in that regard.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The launch of the SGQR code is one positive step in that direction.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Another often heard reservation about the shift towards cashless payments is that people will become desensitised to the value of money and will, therefore, develop reckless spending habits.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such an aversion to e-payments rests on the belief that physically parting with your money gives one the sense of pain and loss and can help instil frugality.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Such concerns, well-founded or otherwise, can be easily addressed with some critical design interventions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Stored value e-wallets already highlight the amount remaining in the account, and provide a helpful log of all recent transactions.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Additional features, such as those allowing users to set a savings target for each month, can also help to nurture good financial habits, including fund management, budgeting and credit management.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Taken together, therefore, all these concerns highlight three salient points of action for addressing consumer resistance to e-payments in general.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, welcome the additional consumer protections introduced by this Bill that will help to shore up consumer confidence and trust in e-payments.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I also look forward to MAS' implementation of the E-Payments User Protection Guidelines at the end of this month.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, however, I would like to ask the Minister whether there will be greater attention paid to (a) enhancing the design of e-payment services so that transactions can be speedier and more intuitive, and (b) addressing concerns about the negative impact of e-payments on personal financial habits.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   To build a Smart Nation, we must rely on technologies to achieve the vision of a cashless society.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to strengthen consumers’ trust and confidence in e-payment.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, we also need to improve the design of e-payment interfaces so that it is easier to use.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to guide the public, especially the elderly, on how to use these apps.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Payment services can generate economic value beyond just transferring money.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, payment services firms use financial data and their customer relationships to provide analytics, business process outsourcing, marketing and credit services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Stripe and Square, two leading United States (US) payment services firms, provide an increasing array of business services to merchants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Payment Services Bill should allow for a competitive market that promotes all types of innovation in payment services, between fintech firms and traditional financial institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After all, Singapore is a small market, but innovations developed here may allow our payment services firms to reach millions of consumers abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are several aspects of the Bill that may affect innovation and competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A firm with only a payment services licence will have to tie-up with a financial institution, or apply for the appropriate licence, to offer credit services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important safeguard because of the risks posed by unregulated consumer lending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, we should also ensure this does not unduly restrict the potential economic value created by payment services firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Consumers and merchants alike may benefit from innovative short-term credit facilities that could be less costly than traditional credit cards and consumer loans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: High frequency consumer payments data may well allow for low-risk small-scale consumer lending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This may be a key area of growth, as Singapore fintech firms expand regionally to reach millions of consumers who now have little access to credit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, section 20 also prohibits payment services licensees from using customer funds from e-money to materially finance their operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While this is an important safeguard, it may also increase the cost of capital for providing e-money services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This issue of the cost of capital is also relevant for section 23, which requires major payment institutions to safeguard customer monies with third-party financial institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While safeguards are vital for public confidence, this may make fintech firms dependent on traditional financial institutions, who are their direct competitors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some respondents to MAS' public consultation on the Payment Services Bill expressed the concern that traditional financial institutions can be hostile to fintech firms, especially where emerging technologies, such as cryptocurrencies, are involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to ask what measures will be taken by MAS to ensure that a competitive market exists for safeguarding services, including directly providing such services as a last resort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Sections 25 to 26 and 51 to 54 on interoperability and the access regime address this problem of barriers to entry created by network effects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Payment services firms operate large consumer and merchant networks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This can be socially beneficial when there are economies of scale, or economies of scope in providing services, such as analytics, marketing or business process outsourcing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But networks obviously also can create barriers to entry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Public discussion of such tests may, in fact, prevent anti-competitive behaviour by payment network operators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Defining the threshold in the Bill to define a licensee as a Major Payment Institution seems somewhat inflexible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to ask if such limits could be defined instead in subsidiary legislation by MAS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the Bill already allows for such flexibility by specifying the section 24 e-wallet transaction limit as a "prescribed amount" to be determined by MAS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to commend MAS for responding to feedback from the public consultation which asked for more flexibility on the e-wallet transaction limits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It will be useful if the Minister could share his thinking on what the initial prescribed amounts for transaction limits are likely to be and the principles behind how regulators will review these limits periodically to support innovation while safeguarding the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A second issue for regulatory flexibility is that as fintech firms become systemically important, their key appointments will be subject to more oversight by MAS regulation on Fit and Proper persons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, some fintech firms have expressed concern whether regulators appreciate the different human capital requirements for key appointment holders between fintech firms and traditional financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is a very comprehensive, well considered, globally researched and, above all, publicly consulted and reviewed.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill commendably sets out to protect Singaporeans in a digitised world.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the Government has been mindful not to immediately overreact and, therefore, over-regulate.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They have seemingly found a way to effectively achieve both outcomes.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With regard to the Bill, firstly, I would like to seek clarification on section 10 on annual fees of licensees.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important distinction from virtual currency which is defined as any digital representation of value that is not denominated in any fiat currency.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In section 3.15 of the MAS Consultation Paper, it is mentioned that "the full definition of virtual currency and e-money are set out in the proposed Bill in Annex B".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I refer to section 19 of the Bill on prohibition against exchanging e-money withdrawn from payment account for Singapore currency.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It seems to be wanting to prohibit exchanging e-money for Singapore currency.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It states under section 19(1)(a), that a licensee that provides an e-money account is to prohibit a customer from (i) withdrawing e-money and (ii) exchanging that e-money "withdrawn" for Singapore currency at any of the licensee’s places of business.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: On this point, can I check why there is a need to exclude an issuer from also doing transactions?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Again, I would like to seek further clarification on the intended outcome that this section is trying to achieve.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In some jurisdictions payment system providers are also able to provide loans and credit facilities to customers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill explicitly forbids such provision of services.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is very hard for a specific country to frame regulations in the digital age of global cross-border businesses.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I feel some of the legislation falls short of this global consideration.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, once again, it is a commendable start for Singapore, who leads the world in framing such forward thinking rules of conduct.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: However, when it comes to innovation, perhaps we can take a leaf from China, specifically WeChat and AliPay.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore was at the forefront of digital innovation, especially for financial innovation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: So, where are we now compared to before?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As a financial hub, we need to keep innovating to stay ahead and to compete globally.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Government’s plan to ensure our financial institutions stay creative and innovative?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Quoting Mr Lim Siong Guan, former Head of Civil Service and former President of the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation, he said, "To ensure the country's continuing success and survival, Singaporeans need to be a people who embrace innovation and excellence and be prepared to go out of their comfort zones, to create a new economic ascent.” We need a culture of innovation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: The spirit of innovation must be made an integral part of our character and personality as a nation and a society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There should be a deliberate, conscious, national effort to get such cultural transformation across all sectors of society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Startups and innovation have become an integral part of culture in countries, such as Finland, Estonia and Israel.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has to get there and be exceptional in our own ways.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This, I believe, should be a cultural change and a mindset change and not simply a case of encouraging innovation.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we are inclined to pile accolades on people who have achieved top grades and got gold medals and leave others unnoticed and unmentioned.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a severe cultural challenge for changing values in society, to value best efforts, as opposed to disproportionately rewarding the super As and gold medalists.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There needs to be far more awareness in society on how to notice and nurture the best efforts of others around us.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It is an intergenerational challenge which needs committed leadership and consistency of effort, behaviour and action.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Rosabeth Moss Kanter of Harvard Business School has pointed out that financial results are a "lagging indicator" of a company’s health. "They tell you what you have just done.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Culture predicts the future." She adds that culture is "more important in some ways than strategy", and that "if you are not thinking about building your culture for survivability and sustainability, then you are not leading".

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: These are strong words, but nonetheless words of wisdom.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that what Prof Kanter says of business applies just as much to nations.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: National culture predicts the course of progress and development of countries.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: To deal with a future which is uncertain and rapidly changing, a culture of innovation is what Singapore needs to build up to be a nation of enterprise and innovation, especially in today's context, where technology and the world move too fast.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill reflects a desire to be innovative but in a suitably cautious manner.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With those words of caution and encouragement, Mr Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The payments landscape has changed considerably with the introduction of various types of payment services.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Payment Services Bill seeks to broaden the scope of regulated activities and allow for separate regulatory frameworks for major payment institutions and smaller players.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, please allow me to highlight a significant area of consideration in the implementation of the said Bill and related regulations.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: These countries were China, Malaysia, India, Pakistan and Indonesia.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, not just the right, but also the smart thing to do for us to be intentional and inclusive of their banking and payment needs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The one million migrant workers on Work Permit rely on payment and remittance services to pay their existing debts and transfer money to their families.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, current options to remit money are limited.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Many work punishing hours with only Sundays off, which they then spend travelling long distances to queue for hours to perform remittances, rather than resting.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While most of us have registered bank accounts with financial intermediaries that afford us an array of payment and e-banking options with fintech, we must not forget the people who do not.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, Iris, a domestic worker from the Philippines.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: She does not have a bank account because: (a) she remits her money in cash, a total of $800 to $1,000, every month at Lucky Plaza to support her two sons in college; and (b) most banks have a prohibitive minimum balance, under which account holders have to pay Fall Below Service Fees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Without a bank account or a digital wallet, Iris is excluded from our financial e-transaction system.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This chips away at the already low wages these workers receive.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: High remittance charges and the lack of remittance options also cause workers to turn to illegal means to remit their money, in addition to the need for money to reach their families urgently in times of emergency.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share the experience of Nayan, a Bangladeshi, who did not resort to these illegal options when he encountered an emergency situation, yet paid a hefty price nonetheless.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Nayan's mother suffered a stroke and needed to be admitted to a city hospital with better facilities.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, he could not remit the money immediately until he completed his basic duty at 4.30 pm before heading to a remittance centre in Farrer Park.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The treatment was, therefore, delayed for his mother, creating implications for her chance of a full recovery.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Further, Nayan had to forgo 5.5 hours of overtime work which resulted in loss of income for him.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure we will all agree that what I have just shared about Iris and Nayan can be called anything but effective.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is the elephant in the room in our quest towards building a Smart Nation, a cashless economy, and an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Work Permit holders can request for electronic payments from employers by law, but many refrain from doing so for fear of job loss and repatriation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, some may, indeed, prefer to receive cash, but many whom I have spoken with do that because they do not know any other trusted options, yet.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mandatory electronic payment of salaries by employers will automatically allow for one million migrant workers to be part of our financial system so they do not remain unbanked or underbanked as rapidly fintech threatens to leave them behind.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This gives them access to more payment and remittance options, lower or zero fees, as well as the benefits of speed and security.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As an illustration of my point, the Post Office Savings Bank's (POSB's) jolly app waives the fee – though it does state for a limited time only, so, hopefully, that stays for a long time – for remittances made to India, Indonesia, Bangladesh and the Philippines but requires employers to open bank accounts for wage payments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: US$5.6 billion is a significant opportunity for the fintech sector to tap into for innovative products in e-payments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The Smart Nation question to ask is: how can we harness this Payment Services Bill to make this opportunity available to the thriving fintech sector if the majority of these funds – the US$5.6 billion – are unbanked or existing outside of the e-payment system?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Traditional financial institutions and newer players are collaborating to bring exciting new fintech products and services to the market, and US$5.6 billion in remittances by migrant workers is definitely one.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We all know the fabled success of Grameen from Bangladesh in financial and social innovation for the unbanked and underbanked.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, if we include our migrant workers fully in our financial system, a fintech equivalent of Grameen from Singapore might just be birthed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, for the many thousands of migrant workers like Iris and Nayan, sending money home – efficiently, reliably and affordably – is a very human activity for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This balance is struck by the calibrated approach taken in applying safeguards relating to standards of consumer protection, anti-money laundering controls, and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond this, the Bill also recognises that regulation may be beneficial, even necessary, for competition and innovation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the 2016 Singapore Payments Roadmap report commissioned by MAS, the limited adoption of electronic payments was attributed to decentralised governance and lack of coordination of infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This suggests that the payment systems market, when left to its own devices, does not lead to the best outcomes for consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill addresses this by providing MAS with regulatory powers relating to interoperability, allowing the regulator to play the role of innovator as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I would like to seek some clarifications and make proposals for the businesses that raise funds through the Initial Coin Offers (ICOs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of the definitions of the various payment services refer to the provision of services to persons in Singapore, but the provider himself does not have to be in Singapore to be required to obtain a licence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, the provision of payment services that affect individuals in Singapore will raise similar risks, whether or not the provider is physically located in Singapore or overseas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, these foreign businesses may already be regulated in their home jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, payment services based in Hong Kong would be subject to the Payment Systems and Stored Value Facilities Ordinance 2015, while those based in the UK are regulated by the Payment Services Regulations 2017.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How would the local regime interact with those of other countries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, would designations under foreign regimes be recognised in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, in the Singapore Payments Roadmap report mentioned earlier, KPMG noted that the lack of interoperability between electronic payment systems was a cause of limited adoption and high costs of electronic payments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Establishing interoperability was a key topic discussed by the Payments Council at its inaugural meeting in August 2017.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill addresses this by providing MAS the powers relating to access regimes, common platforms and common standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 25 and 26 give MAS broad powers to direct that payment service providers ensure interoperability between payment accounts and payment system, and between payment systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Division 4 of Part 3 of the Bill allows MAS to impose access regimes to payment systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Alongside MAS’ regulatory powers, the Payments Council plays an advisory function and is tasked with promoting the interoperability of systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It set up an industry taskforce in August 2017, which developed the SGQR Code to consolidate multiple payment schemes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another agency which is concerned with innovation and competition in the payments industry is the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: CCS has undertaken inquiries into alleged infringements by payment systems, clearing the NETS Affinity Programme of abuse of dominant position in 2007 and clearing Visa’s Multilateral Interchange Fee system of anti-competitive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, CCS had commissioned the New Zealand consultancy company Castalia to study the competitiveness of card payment systems in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how MAS will work with the Payments Council and CCS in exercising its powers relating to interoperability?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, will the Minister look into establishing a regulatory body to exercise specific oversight over competition and innovation for payment systems?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Payment Systems Regulator (PSR) in the UK provides a model for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there is also a general competition regulatory body, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the PSR has a narrower focus on payment systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The co-existence of PSR alongside CMA demonstrates that payment systems give rise to sufficiently unique competition concerns arising from the network effect to require a separate regulatory body.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, section 41 provides that MAS may require participants, operators and settlement institutions to provide information relating to a payment system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes information relating to operations, pricing, participation and any other information that MAS may require for the purposes of the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether this would include information of payment systems users?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, are there any limits on the information that MAS can require?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, would MAS be able to obtain aggregated user data or individually-identifiable information?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also like to raise concerns about the ascendancy of ICOs which accompanied the rise of blockchain and cryptocurrency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: ICO is a method of fundraising used by businesses to build blockchain-centric projects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both statistics indicate that Singapore is favoured by businesses seeking to raise funds through ICOs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I urge MAS to improve its regulatory coverage to build a more robust financial system for the growth of the ICO market.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider the following proposals in future reviews of the payment services regime?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MAS should maintain a central registry of key persons involved in an ICO.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Presently, there is no way for investors to conduct background checks on founders of businesses with an ICO campaign.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such a central registry will help investors easily perform due diligence on their investments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will improve retail investors’ ability to differentiate good projects from scams.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, these businesses are not obliged to provide full disclosure in deployment of funds raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This entails a risk of potential fraud and funds misuse.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: In this regard, the Payment Services Bill is a significant step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: At present, MAS regulates different types of payment services under the PS(O)A (Cap 222A) and the MCRBA (Cap 187).

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: These regulated services include operating payment systems, stored value facilities, remittance business and money-changing services.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Providers of the seven payment services prescribed in the Bill will be required to hold a licence based on the type of payment service that is provided.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The considerable changes to the payment services landscape have brought business models that blur the lines between regulated activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: By combining the PS(O)A and MCRBA, the Bill streamlines these payment services under a single legislative framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: This, in turn, ensures consistent application of laws to various payment activities, which is calibrated at an appropriate level according to the risks the activities pose.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: A consolidated approach also brings greater clarity to the regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: These activities ought to be regulated to ensure adequate controls against ML/TF; provide safeguards against insolvency risks resulting in loss of funds owed to consumers or merchants; reduce fragmentation and limitations to interoperability; and minimise technology and cyber risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The anonymous nature of digital payment token transactions makes them particularly vulnerable to ML/TF risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Moneys received from customers by domestic money transfer and merchant acquisition service providers should be segregated and safeguarded from insolvency risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Different merchant acquisition service providers with a large user base puts interoperability, common standards and accessibility at risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: New payment services that are made possible by technology are just as, if not more, vulnerable to cybersecurity risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: In this respect, the Bill allows MAS to impose risk-mitigating measures and requirements on licensees who conduct the activity that poses the identified risks.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Consequently, gaps in the regulatory regime brought by these new payment services can be filled.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Consumer protection is reinforced, which further engenders public confidence to use the services and encourages development.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Thirdly, the Bill provides MAS with the necessary regulatory flexibility to respond to changes in the fast-moving payments space.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: As a result of the activity-based licensing regime, regulations can be tailored to the risks that specific payment activities pose for different business models.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: In addition, MAS has general powers over all regulated entities, such as powers to conduct inspections and investigations, and emergency powers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: In turn, MAS is able to take a more flexible strategy to target risks as they arise and avoid overregulation that may stifle innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Notably, the Bill gives MAS certain powers to make regulations and supplementary provisions to fulfil the Act’s purposes and amend what would be regulated as a payment service under the Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: This accords MAS the flexibility to modify regulatory scope and come up with new laws for novel and more sophisticated product offerings that may emerge in the future.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: MAS will be able to respond accordingly, such as quickly incorporating new payment activities that ought to be regulated into the regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: This helps to create a conducive environment for innovation, growth and development, without sacrificing consumer protection and stability in the financial system.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: With that, Sir, I end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister-in-charge of MAS, let me now address their questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat was also concerned that services like limited purpose monetary value and loyalty programmes are excluded from the regulatory ambit of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Bill governs the provision of payment services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the issuance of stored value cards like EZ-Link card or NETS cashcard that can be used to pay for various goods and services will be regulated as a type of payment service, and customer monies in those cards will be protected under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, limited purpose monetary value like supermarket shopping vouchers and loyalty programmes like airline frequent flyer miles, cannot ordinarily be used to pay for goods and services provided by unrelated third parties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Likewise, prepayments to bike sharing platforms for their services are also not payment services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, all these activities are excluded from the ambit of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is the approach taken by jurisdictions, such as Australia, Hong Kong and the UK, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On a technical point, Mr Mohamed Irshad asked for the location of e-money and virtual currency definitions in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These terms are defined in the interpretation clause of the Bill but we have changed the term "virtual currency" to "digital payment token" (DPT) instead, to accurately reflect the nature of these units as tokens and not currency.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Louis Ng asked about customer protection in cryptocurrency services and for ICOs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We also need to be mindful of what Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out, which is, regulating DPT services for customer protection can have a legitimising effect, when digital tokens are still in a nascent stage of development.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This may send the wrong signal that Singapore is promoting or welcoming such activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because we are regulating it, it actually gives people comfort that this is a legitimate activity and gives the public false comfort that their DPT investments are safe.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Similarly, running a registration system for ICOs, as Mr Louis Ng suggested, can also have a similar "legitimising" effect.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS is monitoring this space and will continue to put out consumer advisories aimed at preventing investment losses upfront.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS also continually updates its Investors Alert List to include entities that have been misperceived as being regulated by MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In this regard, Deputy Prime Minister Tharman has also made it clear in Parliament earlier last year that DPTs, like bitcoins, are a very high-risk investment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To adequately caution investors, MAS will require DPT service providers to disclose clearly to their customers that their investment is not subject to regulatory protection.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we would consider penalties for fraud and misuse of funds raised by ICO issuers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are existing penalties for such illegal activities and they are administered by the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun, Mr Leon Perera and Mr Louis Ng pointed out that consumer protection should also extend to consumer education.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun proposed public education to communicate the advantages of using e-payments and good personal financial habits.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat expressed that we should include senior citizens and the less tech-savvy among us in our e-payments journey.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Through MoneySENSE, the national financial education programme, MAS has been working to raise public awareness on using e-payments safely and responsibly and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The public sector is also raising citizens' digital literacy and familiarity with new technologies, through initiatives, such as IMDA's digital inclusion programme, and the SkillsFuture for Digital Workplace programme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On financial inclusion, Ms Anthea Ong highlighted the difficulties faced by migrant workers in accessing e-payment solutions and bank accounts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As she noted, payment firms are collaborating to bring new fintech products to the market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, fintech has enabled us to remit money overseas via e-wallets.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are easy to use, usually free, with no minimum balances required.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As this Bill strengthens safeguards for these payment services, we should see greater adoption from consumers, including migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the same time, banks are working on enhancing financial inclusion for migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, POSB has partnered the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) to enable foreign domestic workers to open bank accounts seamlessly when they submit their online Work Permit applications.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The initial deposit is waived for these POSB Payroll Accounts which also provide low-cost remittance services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
