text: This is not just that this is a US$5.6 billion market, but this is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Next, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about business competitiveness, and said that financial institutions should not be overly burdened by new rules.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They asked how the Bill compares to those in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In other jurisdictions, these risks are addressed by different authorities under different pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As explained in my speech earlier, MAS has consciously balanced mitigating risk with promoting innovation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The best way to do this is to avoid a one-size-fits-all approach, and instead adopt a risk-based approach, such that the regulatory requirements are commensurate with the risks of the business activities, and that is why we have three licence classes in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the Second Reading speech, I explained how a major payment institution can provide services above specified thresholds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked why the thresholds are not in the subsidiary legislation and in the main Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, specifying thresholds in the subsidiary legislation – it is actually easier for MAS – it gives us flexibility and more administrative ease but, to the market, it may mean less certainty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS can still amend it, through this House, should we need to in future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Regarding transitional arrangements and if 12 months was sufficient, in the public consultation, almost all entities who asked for a longer transition period requested a 12-month period, and so MAS agreed that this is a sensible timeline.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat correctly noted that Singapore has been fully supportive of the G20 and FATF.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Taking our AML/CFT commitment seriously is something we must do, to maintain the integrity and reputation of our financial system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, we will take care to calibrate our AML/CFT measures using a risk-based approach, too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will consult the industry with the proposed measures to ensure that the measures are risk-appropriate and fit-for-purpose.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if MAS has powers to obtain information of individual payment system users from private entities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As a regulatory and enforcement agency like all others, MAS has such powers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But like all the other enforcement and regulatory agencies, we will exercise them judiciously, for the purposes of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, MAS may require demographics of individual users to determine any gaps in access to payment services by any particular population segment, or we may request for such data for the purpose of investigation of a breach of law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Leon Perera also asked about the rationale and considerations for arriving at the proposed stock and flow caps on personal e-money accounts, and if these limits could be prohibitive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have explained the rationale for having the caps in my Second Reading speech, and that this is important to preserve stability of the financial system to prevent a significant outflow from the banking system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, most e-money issuers have self-imposed stock caps of less than $1,000.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, based on data from the last Household Expenditure Survey conducted and after adjusting for annual growth rates, the average monthly and annual household expenditure per household member in the 61st to 80th percentile group, is around $2,000 and $24,000 respectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The proposed amounts, therefore, provide sufficient headroom for most individuals, even if they were to pay all their expenses of the month out of one e-money account.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nonetheless, these are initial numbers, and we can review over time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And as suggested by Mr Leon Perera, MAS is also prepared to grant exemptions by way of regulations to facilitate specific customer needs.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS will soon be consulting on the regulations and will consider any further industry feedback.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira also asked something about fit and proper checks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The tech industry can be assured that this is a nascent industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do understand, for fintech companies, the founders are often of technology background.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we also recognise that as they grow, as they serve bigger customers and become a bigger institution, they also start to recruit more diverse talents into their home, into their leadership team, including those with banking and financial service experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is an evolving criterion, and MAS will constantly review that to make sure they keep up with the times.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are other measures that MAS will set out in subsidiary legislation that will be published for consultation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These include the annual fees that Mr Mohamed Irshad asked about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These also include the measures that Mr Leon Perera and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about, such as the obligations for disclosures to end customers, and the steps that standard payment institutions must take when they exceed specific thresholds for their licence class, including suitable grace periods and the need in order to be upgraded to a higher licence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will take all Members' comments into account regarding the specificity of the disclosure with customers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how MAS intends to enforce provisions against foreign established licensees and whether foreign regulated payment firms would be recognised in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat has provided feedback that payment service providers, including DPT exchanges or service providers, have had their bank accounts closed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should clarify that most payment service providers do not have problems opening and maintaining corporate accounts with banks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To help firms that have faced such difficulties, MAS has been facilitating discussions among banks, fintech firms and DPT service providers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While MAS does not intervene in the commercial decisions of financial institutions, such discussions should lead to positive and meaningful outcomes.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are a number of questions on the limitations of activities of payment service providers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out that Hong Kong has a more liberal regime and is considering to allow payment services providers to offer banking services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What Hong Kong is doing is to issue digital banking licences, with regulatory requirements that are much higher than pure e-payment services firms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Singapore, banks, too, can opt for a fully digital business model.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Indeed, today, Singapore residents can already open a bank account with any of the local banks and operate it without having to visit a branch.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The real question is whether there are benefits for Singapore to increase the number of banks in Singapore by admitting primarily digital startup banks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is a broader banking policy that has to be studied carefully, and quite distinct from the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira, Mr Mohamed Irshad and Mr Leon Perera all asked about cash withdrawal and lending measures for licensees.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the Second Reading speech, I explained why we are not prepared for licensees to offer such services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Essentially, these are core functions of banks which have a unique economic role.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They take in deposits and then on-lend to the economy, as I have explained in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To allow e-payment service providers, which are subject to much lower thresholds and a much lower regulatory regime, to be able to provide lending activities, undermines the position and role of the banks; and, too, likewise, for the thresholds that they can hold in the stock and cap.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have not extended the same prohibition to cash withdrawal from non-resident e-wallets as Mr Leon Perera pointed out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This partly facilitates tourists' spending but, more importantly, the non-resident e-wallets draw on the bank deposits from other countries and do not affect our banking system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is also not just a matter of FTA compliance, but also a broader consideration for our banking stability.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are still learning about this whole industry, how it is evolving.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But banks are an important part of our economy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are taking quite a cautious approach at this moment, and the situation will continue to evolve and we have to consider it as time evolves.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad also asked about what plans the Government has to encourage innovation by financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To encourage innovation in financial services, we have the MAS regulatory sandbox.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The sandbox is open to all firms that wish to experiment with a technologically innovative solution in financial services within MAS' regulatory ambit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MAS has proposed the creation of predefined sandboxes known as the Sandbox Express – easier and faster to get in and to get out.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members also asked about Singapore's payment ecosystem and the competitive landscape of the industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if there should be a dedicated regulatory authority to oversee competition and innovation in the payment space.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is not necessary for us, because between MAS and CCS, we will cover the issues on competition in payment services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have found this collaborative approach suitable to address any competition issues that may arise in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira also asked how MAS will ensure a competitive market exist for safeguarding services of fintech firms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is actually quite a competitive service for the banks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Major financial institutions are also familiar with the standard of behaviour in the Singapore market, and we will not hesitate to act on complaints regarding any anti-competitive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for the thresholds to enforce against anti-competitive behaviour, this is actually quite an involved process.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It depends on the service, the players in the service, the size of the companies, the industry structure and the value chain.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Each case is different and regulators have to make a fairly laborious determination based on the facts and the alleged anti-competitive behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked when we can have a common e-payment platform and whether merchants affected by interoperability measures can expect assistance from MAS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We then take steps to ensure open architecture and interoperability between different payment systems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, we enhance ease of use and convenience for consumers and merchants while allowing and promoting competition in the space.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we very much share the wishes of Prof Lim Sun Sun, while being cognisant of the risks in a small market like ours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With all these in place today, I hope all of us, as consumers, also can realise how e-payment is functioning today compared to, say, a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is actually quite easy to use now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: E-payments can be made through a simple tap-and-go of your credit or debit contactless card, or your smartphone on a Unified Point of Service (UPOS) terminal.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sending money to your friend can be done quite easily with a few taps on your smartphone.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With time, I am confident that e-payments will be even simpler to use, and more consumers will grow to trust and accept e-payments.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, let us say, a non-bank e-wallet joins FAST, what it means is that I can transfer my non-bank e-wallet money to my bank account and from my bank account, I can withdraw the money.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our standing is not too bad at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are a city-state, unlike the US, China or even Indonesia with a huge market.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are a well-regulated financial hub, and we ensure fintech companies can operate in an environment full of opportunities and with certainty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our annual Fintech Festival is the largest in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not plan it to be the largest, but they turned out to be the largest because fintech firms want to come here so that they can network and promote their services to the financial industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And for the fintech firms, it is especially in view that they could promote their services to the large financial institutions and global institutions which are here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, supporting the growth of major financial institutions and fintech startups is, therefore, not a zero-sum game.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are all part of the financial ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Understanding that, and taking a risk-focused, modular approach to regulation, will contribute meaningfully to Singapore's innovation culture.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I understand Mr Mohamed Irshad's broader points on culture and mindset.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do agree with many of the points he raised but those are beyond the ambit of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At some point, perhaps during an education debate, I will be more than happy to address some of the issues the Member raised.
